questions.q: What does it mean for communication between two systems to be synchronous?
options: The caller sends a request and blocks, waiting for a response, before it continues doing anything else
The two systems never exchange data directly
The caller sends a request and immediately moves on without expecting any response
Data is only exchanged once per day on a fixed schedule
questions.explain: Synchronous communication means the caller stops and waits for a response before proceeding — the defining trait that distinguishes it from asynchronous patterns covered in the next lesson.

questions.q: What is the central trade-off synchronous communication makes, per this lesson?
options: It always uses less network bandwidth than asynchronous communication
It guarantees the called system will always respond within one second
It couples the calling system's performance and availability to the called system's performance and availability
It removes the need for any authentication between systems
questions.explain: Because the caller blocks and waits, its own performance becomes dependent on how fast and how available the called system is — a dependency the caller doesn't fully control.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of callouts a single Apex transaction can make, and what is the cumulative callout timeout cap across that transaction?
options: 10 callouts per transaction, no cumulative cap
100 callouts per transaction, with a 120-second cumulative timeout cap across all callouts in the transaction
1,000 callouts per transaction, with a 10-second cumulative cap
There is no limit on the number of callouts per transaction, only on individual callout timeout
questions.explain: Salesforce caps a single Apex transaction at 100 callouts, with cumulative callout time across the whole transaction capped at 120 seconds — additive across every callout the transaction makes, per Salesforce's Apex Developer Guide.

questions.q: Which scenario from this lesson is the strongest example of a business process that genuinely needs a synchronous answer?
options: Logging an order to an external system for a newsletter segment with no downstream dependency on success
Archiving old records to cold storage once a quarter
Sending a nightly summary report to a data warehouse
A real-time inventory check that must complete before an order can be confirmed
questions.explain: A real-time inventory check genuinely blocks the business process — the order can't be confirmed without an answer right now — unlike logging or archiving, which don't need to hold up the triggering transaction.

questions.q: What anti-pattern does this lesson warn against regarding synchronous callouts from Apex triggers?
options: Making a synchronous callout to log an event or kick off a downstream process that has no actual dependency on the triggering transaction's own success
Using synchronous callouts for payment authorization before checkout
Ever using Apex triggers for any integration work
Using asynchronous patterns for any time-sensitive integration
questions.explain: Needlessly coupling a transaction to another system's availability for a callout with no real business dependency — such as logging an event — is an unexamined default, not a deliberate design choice, and it's exactly the kind of decision an architect should question.
